newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian police block marches by 70,000 protesters.
newsitem.headline: Serbian police block marches by 70,000 protesters.

text.p: Serbian security police blocked marches by 70,000 people in Belgrade on Sunday in the 42nd straight day of protests in a crisis over local election results.

Some 50,000 activists of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition and 20,000 students massed in Belgrade squares at different times and then tried to swarm into major streets only to run into walls of riot police.
Both protest columns were boxed in by police cordons and had to retreat into pedestrian lanes or side streets. No disturbances were reported before demonstrators dispersed.

Police were enforcing a ban on street marches imposed by the ruling Socialist party (SPS) after a December 24 riot involving Zajedno protesters and government loyalists driven into Belgrade to champion President Slobodan Milosevic.
Zajedno said one of their supporters died of his injuries after being trampled to death by comrades trying to flee a police charge in the Christmas Eve brawl.
Sunday's protesters took the police blockades in their stride. They walked in circles as if they were imprisoned and shouted "Murderers" and "Dogs" at police.
A carnival atmosphere then set in with demonstrators linking hands in dances to Serbian folk music.

Up to a quarter of a million people have demonstrated in the Belgrade protests. There have also been other demonstrations across Serbia against the SPS's annulment of November 17 municipal elections won by the loose Zajedno bloc.
The SPS cited unspecified "irregularities" in the polling.

But Zajedno, supported later by findings of a special mission from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), accused the SPS of vote-rigging and wants its victories reinstated in 14 major towns and cities including Belgrade.
Western governments have warned Milosevic he can forget about financial aid for his wrecked economy unless he concedes electoral defeats and starts broad democratic reform.

Milosevic, determined to extend 50 years of unbroken rule by his party but loath to burn bridges to the West partially rebuilt after war-related U.N. sanctions were lifted, was expected to respond to the OSCE report in the coming week.
There have been hints of compromise from some quarters of the government. Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic described the OSCE verdict as "considered and balanced".

But analysts say SPS hardliners who lead privileged lives from their control of state enterprises and shrug off the spectre of renewed ostracism by the West are pressing Milosevic to draw a line in the sand against Zajedno now.
They want to reassert the SPS's domination of the political agenda before parliamentary and presidential elections in 1997.
A Zajedno statement accused Milosevic of adopting an undeclared state of emergency to throttle protests. It claimed police were flooding key provincial cities to scare Zajedno.
A rally planned in the northern provincial town of Smederevska Palanka on Sunday was cancelled after police banned it without explanation, an opposition statement said.
But university students rallied without interference in the second largest Serbian city Nis, wearing shooting targets on their heads in anger at police assaults in Belgrade.
Vuk Draskovic, a Zajedno leader, said the opposition was prepared to hold talks with Milosevic if he accepted the November election outcome.

But in a speech to opposition marchers carried live by independent B-92 radio, Draskovic said that if Milosevic refused to recognise the poll results, Zajedno would withdraw its deputies from all assemblies where results were annulled.
"We must be wise, determined, and they (SPS) will fall, maybe in a month, maybe two, but they will fall," he said.

Opposition rallies were peaceful and good-humoured until Milosevic drafted 40,000 loyalists from the provinces into Belgrade on December 24 to confront Zajedno. Some 50 people were injured in the ensuing melee.
